newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia kicks out politicians in corruption drive.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia kicks out politicians in corruption drive.

text.p: Two Malaysian state politicians were sacked for alleged corruption on Friday joining a federal deputy minister sacked earlier in the week.

Mohamed Aini Taib, the second-ranking executive in the central state of Selangor was dropped from the state's executive committee, along with another member, S.S. Rajagopal, as the heat built up on a government campaign against corruption.

Aini, the Selangor executive, was barred from contesting a Supreme Council seat in last year's UMNO party elections after the leadership accused him of "money politics", which covers a host of sins, including vote buying.

The dismissals came after Deputy Primary Industries Minister Siti Zainab Abu Bakar was sacked on Thursday. Zainab was also suspended as a member of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's United Malays National Organisation (UMNO).
Zainab and parliament senator Habshah Osman, whose UMNO membership was also suspended, were accused of diverting 1.8 million ringgit ($717,000) from the UMNO women's wing accounts.
Siti was its former treasurer and Habshah a former secretary.

"We must take action if we want to cleanse the party and government from black sheep and do not want corruption to be part of our culture or a disease which can erode people's confidence," UMNO vice-president Najib Razak said on Friday.
Najib, also Malaysia's Education Minister, said the sackings will send a "loud and clear" signal to corrupt members.

On Monday, a lawmaker from west coast Malacca state was charged with allegedly abusing his position in approving state land for a commercial development, while an aide to the late chief minister of that state was accused in court of accepting a Mercedes Benz to expedite approval of an investment project.

Sahar Arpan, the lawmaker in the Malacca land case, faces a maximum 14 years imprisonment and fine of 20,000 ringgit, while Azman Ghani, the political aide accused of accepting the Mercedes, is liable to two years jail, if convicted, prosecutors said. Sahar and Azman pleaded not guilty.
Heavier penalties were also passed against corruption last week, with the maximum jail sentence being doubled to 10 years while maximum fines were raised 10-fold to 100,000 ringgit.
The opposition showered rare praise on the government, but demanded more transparency and consistency in the action.

"It has made me dare to hope for the first time in three decades that there is a possibility that the government may embark on an all-out war against corruption in high political places," opposition leader Lim Kit Siang said.
But the Democratic Action Party chief said the campaign must continue indefinitely as "a swallow does not make a summer".
Parti Rakyat Malaysia (PRM), another opposition group, urged the government to act next on an alleged mismanagement scandal in Malaysian state steelmaker Perwaja.

The former managing director of the company Eric Chia, handpicked by Prime Minister Mahathir, resigned before the scandal broke out. Perwaja, which is in the midst of being privatised had accummulated losses of $1.2 billion.

The PRM compared the Perwaja case with the swift action taken by South Korean authorities on the scandal in their national steel company Hanbo. "It puts us to shame," PRM president Syed Hussain Ali said.

Financial market analysts speculated that Prime Minister Mahathir had planned the crackdown to coincide with his two-month leave in Europe, with Deputy Prime Minister Anwar formally given charge of both the government and UMNO.
In a video conference link-up from London on Thursday, Mahathir urged the UMNO leadership "to support this and any future decisions on this matter just as the Cabinet has done".
($1 = 2.51 ringgit)
